column2: And when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
then Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus,
bound fair sandals under his feet,
and took a valiant spear that fitted his palm,
eager for the city, and spoke to his swineherd:

Father, I am going to the city, so that my mother
7	may see me; for I do not think she will cease
8	from hateful weeping and tearful lament
9	before she sees me myself; and to you I give this charge.
10	Lead this unlucky stranger to the city, that there
11	he may beg a meal; and whoever wishes will give him
12	a loaf and a cup; and I cannot possibly put up with all
13	men, having pains in my heart;
14	and if the stranger is very angry, it will be the worse
15	for him; for I like to speak the truth.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Friend, I myself do not wish to be kept back;
18	it is better for a beggar to beg a meal in the city than in the fields;
19	and whoever wishes will give to me.
20	For I am no longer of an age to stay at the farmsteads,
21	so as to obey everything when a master gives orders.
22	But go; this man will lead me, whom you bid,
23	as soon as I have warmed myself at the fire and the sun is hot.
24	For I have terribly bad clothes here; lest the morning
25	frost overcome me; and you say the city is far off.
So he spoke, and Telemachus went through the farmstead,
striding with swift feet, and was devising evils for the suitors.
And when he reached the well-inhabited house,
he set his spear, bringing it, against a tall pillar,
and himself went inside and crossed the stone threshold.
Far the first to see him was the nurse Eurycleia,
spreading fleeces on the richly wrought chairs,
and weeping she ran straight to him; and about him the other
maidservants of patient Odysseus gathered,
and kissed, embracing, his head and shoulders.
And prudent Penelope came out of her chamber,
like Artemis or golden Aphrodite,
and threw her arms about her dear son, weeping,
and kissed his head and both his fair eyes,
and lamenting spoke winged words:

You have come, Telemachus, sweet light. I did not think
42	I should see you again, when you went in the ship to Pylos
43	secretly, against my will, to hear news of your dear father.
44	But come, tell me how you met with the sight.
And discreet Telemachus answered her:

My mother, do not stir up lament in me nor rouse my heart
47	in my breast, who have just escaped sheer destruction;
48	but bathe, and taking clean clothes for your skin,
49	go up to the upper chamber with your attendant women
50	and pray to all the gods to offer perfect hecatombs,
51	in case Zeus may somewhere bring about deeds of requital.
52	And I shall go to the assembly, to invite
53	a stranger, who followed me from there as I came here.
54	I sent him ahead with my godlike comrades,
55	and I bade Piraeus take him to his house
56	and treat him kindly and honour him, until I come.
So he spoke, and for her the word was wingless.
And she bathed, and taking clean clothes for her skin,
prayed to all the gods to offer perfect hecatombs,
in case Zeus may somewhere bring about deeds of requital.
And Telemachus went through the hall
holding his spear; and with him two swift-footed dogs followed.
And Athena poured marvellous grace upon him;
and all the people marvelled at him as he approached.
And around him the proud suitors gathered,
speaking fair words, but in their minds plotting evil.
But he avoided the great throng of them,
and where Mentor sat and Antiphus and Halitherses,
who from the beginning were his father's comrades,
there he went and sat down; and they asked about each thing.
And near them came Piraeus, famed for his spear,
bringing the stranger to the assembly through the city; and not long
did Telemachus turn aside far from the stranger, but stood by him.
And Piraeus spoke first to him:

Telemachus, quickly send women to my house,
76	that I may send you the gifts that Menelaus gave you.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

Piraeus, we do not know how these matters will be.
79	If the proud suitors in the halls
80	kill me secretly and divide all my father's goods,
81	I wish that you rather than any of these should have and enjoy them;
82	but if I devise slaughter and doom for these men,
83	then bring them gladly to my house, to me rejoicing.
So saying, he led the hard-tried stranger to the house.
And when they came to the well-inhabited house,
they laid their cloaks on the couches and chairs,
and going into the polished baths they bathed.
And when the maidservants had washed them and anointed them with oil,
and cast woollen cloaks and tunics about them,
they went out of the baths and sat on couches.
A handmaid poured water for the hands from a jug, bringing it
in a fair golden one, over a silver basin,
to wash; and she drew up a polished table beside.
And the revered housekeeper brought bread and set it by,
adding many dishes, giving freely of what was there.
And his mother sat opposite by the pillar of the hall,
leaning on a couch, spinning fine yarn.
And they put out their hands to the food ready laid before them.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
prudent Penelope began to speak among them:

Telemachus, I shall go up to the upper chamber
102	and lie down in my bed, which has become a place of groaning,
103	always drenched with my tears, since Odysseus
104	went away with the sons of Atreus to Ilios; and you did not dare,
105	before the proud suitors came to this house,
106	to tell me plainly of your father's return, if you heard anything.
And discreet Telemachus answered her:

Well then, mother, I shall tell you the truth.
109	We went to Pylos and to Nestor, shepherd of the people;
110	and he received me in his high house
111	and treated me kindly, as a father his son
112	who has come after a long time, new from elsewhere; so he
113	treated me kindly with his glorious sons.
114	But of patient Odysseus he said he had never
115	heard from any man on earth, alive or dead;
116	but he sent me on to the son of Atreus, Menelaus famed for his spear,
117	with horses and a well-fitted chariot.
118	There I saw Argive Helen, for whose sake many
119	Argives and Trojans toiled by the gods' will.
120	And at once Menelaus, good at the war-cry, asked
121	what need had brought me to divine Lacedaemon;
122	and I told him the whole truth;
123	and then he answered me and said:
124	'Alas, indeed they wished to lie in the bed of a man
125	of stout heart, being themselves feeble.
126	As when in a thicket a hind has laid to sleep
127	her newborn suckling fawns in the lair of a strong lion,
128	and goes searching the slopes and grassy glens
129	grazing, and then he enters his lair,
130	and sends a shameful fate on both of them,
131	so Odysseus will send a shameful fate on those men.
132	Would that, father Zeus and Athena and Apollo,
133	being such as once in well-built Lesbos
134	he rose up in a quarrel and wrestled with Philomeleides,
135	and threw him mightily, and all the Achaeans rejoiced,
136	such a one Odysseus might meet the suitors;
137	all would be short-lived and bitter in their marriage.
138	But what you ask me and entreat, I would not
139	say otherwise, evading, nor deceive you,
140	but what the old man of the sea, the unerring, told me,
141	of that I shall hide no word from you nor conceal it.
142	He said he saw him on an island suffering strong pains,
143	in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him
144	by force; and he cannot reach his fatherland.
145	For he has no ships with oars and no comrades
146	to send him over the broad back of the sea.'
147	So spoke the son of Atreus, Menelaus famed for his spear.
148	Having done this I returned; and the immortals gave me a wind,
149	who quickly sent me to my dear fatherland.
So he spoke, and stirred her heart in her breast.
And among them spoke also godlike Theoclymenus:

O revered wife of Odysseus son of Laertes,
153	he does not know clearly; but attend to my word;
154	for I shall prophesy to you exactly and shall not hide it.
155	Let Zeus be witness first of the gods, and the hospitable table
156	and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come,
157	that Odysseus is indeed already in his fatherland,
158	sitting or creeping, learning of these evil deeds,
159	and devises evil for all the suitors;
160	such an omen I saw as I sat on the well-benched ship,
161	and I called it out to Telemachus.
And prudent Penelope answered him:
So they spoke such things to one another,
and the suitors before the hall of Odysseus
were amusing themselves with discs and throwing javelins,
on the levelled ground, where they had been before in their insolence.
But when it was suppertime, and the flocks came
from the fields on every side, and those drove them who did before,
then Medon spoke to them—for he most of all the heralds
pleased them, and was present at their feasts:
So he spoke, and they stood up and went, obeying his word.
And when they came to the well-inhabited house,
they laid their cloaks on the couches and chairs,
and they sacrificed great sheep and fat goats,
and sacrificed fat swine and a cow of the herd,
preparing the feast. And from the country to the city
Odysseus and the divine swineherd were hastening to go.
And among them the swineherd, leader of men, began to speak:

Stranger, since you are eager to go to the city
186	today, as my lord ordered—though I myself
187	would rather leave you here as guardian of the farmsteads;
188	but I respect and fear him, lest afterwards
189	he reproach me; and harsh are the rebukes of masters—
190	but come now let us go; for the day has largely
191	passed, and soon toward evening it will be colder for you.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

I understand, I take heed; you bid one who understands.
194	But let us go, and you lead all the way.
195	And give me, if you have anywhere a cut staff,
196	to lean on, since you say the path is slippery.
He spoke, and threw about his shoulders his mean wallet,
full of holes; and in it was a twisted rope for a strap;
and Eumaeus gave him a staff to his liking.
The two went, and the dogs and herdsmen
stayed behind and guarded the farmstead; and he led his lord to the city
like a wretched old beggar,
leaning on a staff; and he wore wretched clothes on his skin.
But when going along the rugged road
they were near the town and came to the spring
built, fair-flowing, from which the townspeople drew water,
which Ithacus and Neritus and Polyctor made;
and around it was a grove of water-nourished poplars,
all round in a circle, and cold water flowed down
from a rock above; and above it an altar had been made
to the nymphs, where all wayfarers sacrificed.
There Melanthius son of Dolius met them,
driving goats, which were the best among all the herds,
a dinner for the suitors; and two herdsmen followed him.
And seeing them he rebuked them and spoke a word and addressed them,
terrible and shameful; and he stirred the heart of Odysseus:

Now indeed, an utter rogue leads a rogue,
218	as always the god leads like to like.
219	Where do you lead this filthy fellow, wretched swineherd,
220	an irksome beggar, a spoiler of feasts?
221	Who, standing at many doorposts, will rub his shoulders,
222	begging for scraps, not swords or cauldrons;
223	if you would give him to me to be keeper of my farmsteads
224	and sweeper of the folds and carrier of fodder for the kids,
225	drinking whey he would put on a great thigh.
226	But since he has learned bad ways, he will not wish
227	to go to work, but cowering through the land
228	he wants to feed his insatiable belly by begging.
229	But I tell you, and it will be fulfilled:
230	if he comes to the house of divine Odysseus,
231	many footstools from men's hands about his head
232	will fly past, and rub his ribs as he is pelted through the house.
So he spoke, and coming up kicked him in his folly
on the hip; but he did not push him from the path,
but stood firm; and Odysseus pondered
whether to rush at him and take his life with the club,
or lift him by the middle and dash his head to the ground.
But he endured, and restrained himself in his mind; and the swineherd
rebuked him to his face, and prayed aloud, lifting up his hands:

Nymphs of the spring, daughters of Zeus, if ever Odysseus
241	burned thigh-pieces to you, covering them with rich fat,
242	of lambs and kids, fulfil this wish for me:
243	that that man may come, and a god lead him;
244	then he would scatter all your finery,
245	which you now wear, insolent, always wandering
246	through the town; and bad herdsmen ruin the flocks.
And again Melanthius, goatherd of goats, said to him:

Alas, what a thing he has said, the dog who knows destructive tricks,
249	whom I one day on a well-benched black ship
250	shall take far from Ithaca, that he may fetch me much livelihood.
251	Would that silver-bowed Apollo might strike Telemachus
252	today in the halls, or that he be subdued by the suitors,
253	as for Odysseus the day of return has perished far away.
So saying he left them there walking slowly,
and he went and very quickly reached the house of his lord.
At once he went in, and sat among the suitors,
opposite Eurymachus; for him he loved most.
Before him those who worked put a portion of meat,
and the revered housekeeper brought bread and set it by him
to eat. And close by Odysseus and the divine swineherd
stopped as they came, and around them came the sound
of the hollow lyre; for Phemius was beginning to sing for them;
and Odysseus, taking the swineherd by the hand, said:

Eumaeus, surely this is the fair house of Odysseus,
265	and easily recognized, and to be seen among many.
266	One part follows another, and its courtyard is furnished
267	with wall and coping, and the doors are well defended,
268	double; no man could despise it.
269	And I know that many men are holding a feast in it,
270	since the savour of fat rises from it, and in it the lyre
271	sounds, which the gods made the companion of the feast.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

You recognized it easily, since you are not witless in other matters either.
274	But come, let us consider how these things shall be.
275	Either you go in first to the well-inhabited house
276	and join the suitors, and I shall remain here;
277	or, if you wish, wait, and I shall go before;
278	but do not delay, lest someone seeing you outside
279	either strike or drive you off; and I bid you consider this.
And then much-enduring divine Odysseus answered him:

I understand, I take heed; you bid one who understands.
282	But go before, and I shall remain here.
283	For I am not unacquainted with blows or missiles;
284	my spirit is enduring, since I have suffered many evils
285	in waves and in war; let this too be added to them.
286	But the ravening belly it is not possible to hide,
287	accursed, which gives many evils to men,
288	for whose sake well-benched ships too are equipped
289	over the barren sea, bearing evils to enemies.
So they spoke such things to one another;
and a dog, lying there, raised his head and ears,
Argos, of patient Odysseus, whom once he himself
had reared, but had no joy of him, before he went to sacred Ilios.
In former days young men used to take him
after wild goats and deer and hares;
but now he lay neglected, his master gone,
in a great heap of dung, which before the doors
of mules and cattle lay in plenty, until the servants of Odysseus
should carry it out to manure the great estate;
there lay the dog Argos, full of dog-ticks.
Then, when he perceived Odysseus was near,
he wagged his tail and dropped both his ears,
but no nearer could he any more come
to his master; and he, looking away, wiped off a tear,
easily escaping Eumaeus's notice, and at once asked with a word:

Eumaeus, truly it is a wonder, this dog lies in the dung.
307	He is fair in form, but this I do not clearly know,
308	whether with this beauty he was also swift in running,
309	or is just like table-dogs of men,
310	which their masters keep for show.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Indeed this is the dog of a man who died far away.
313	If he were such in form and in deeds
314	as Odysseus left him when he went to Troy,
315	you would soon marvel, seeing his speed and strength.
316	For nothing escaped him in the depths of the deep wood
317	of any beast he pursued; for he was keen also on the track.
318	But now he is in an evil plight, and his master has perished
319	elsewhere than his fatherland, and the careless women do not tend him.
320	And servants, when masters no longer have power,
321	no longer wish to do what is right;
322	for wide-seeing Zeus takes away half of a man's
323	virtue, when the day of slavery seizes him.
So saying he went into the well-inhabited house,
and went straight to the hall, to the noble suitors.
And Argos the fate of black death seized,
as soon as he saw Odysseus in the twentieth year.
And far the first to see the swineherd coming
through the house was godlike Telemachus, and quickly then
he nodded to him, calling him; and he, looking round, took a stool
which lay where the carver sat, carving much meat
for the suitors feasting in the house;
this he carried and set by Telemachus's table
opposite, and sat down there himself; and for him the herald
took a portion and set it, and lifted bread from a basket.
And close behind him Odysseus entered the house,
like a wretched old beggar,
leaning on a staff; and he wore wretched clothes on his skin.
He sat on the ash-wood threshold inside the doors,
leaning on a cypress post, which a carpenter once
skilfully smoothed and made straight to the line.
And Telemachus called the swineherd to him and said,
taking a whole loaf from the beautiful basket
and meat, as much as his hands could hold in his grasp:
So he spoke, and the swineherd went, when he heard the word,
and standing near spoke winged words:
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Lord Zeus, may Telemachus be fortunate among men,
355	and may he have all that he desires in his mind.
He spoke, and received it with both hands and put it down
there before his feet, on his mean wallet,
and ate while the singer sang in the halls;
when he had dined, then the divine singer ceased.
The suitors made an uproar through the hall. But Athena,
standing near Odysseus son of Laertes,
urged him to gather scraps of bread among the suitors,
and learn which of them were righteous and which lawless;
but not even so was she going to save any one from evil.
He went to ask each man, going from left to right,
holding out his hand on every side, as if he had long been a beggar.
And they, pitying, gave, and marvelled at him,
and asked one another who he was and where he came from.
And among them spoke Melanthius, goatherd of goats:

Hear me, suitors of the very famous queen,
371	about this stranger; for I have seen him before.
372	Indeed the swineherd led him here,
373	but of him I do not clearly know from where he claims descent.
So he spoke, and Antinous rebuked the swineherd with words:

O notorious swineherd, why did you bring this man
376	to the city? Are there not enough wanderers for us, and others,
377	irksome beggars, spoilers of feasts?
378	Do you think it a small thing that they devour your lord's livelihood
379	gathering here, and you have called this man too?
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Antinous, you do not speak fair, though you are noble;
382	for who himself goes and calls a stranger from elsewhere,
383	another, unless it is one of those who are workers for the people,
384	a seer or a healer of ills or a builder of timbers,
385	or even a divine singer, who gives delight with his song?
386	For these are invited over the boundless earth;
387	but a beggar no one would call to wear him out.
388	But always you above all the suitors are harsh
389	to the servants of Odysseus, and most of all to me; but I
390	do not care, as long as prudent Penelope
391	lives in the halls and godlike Telemachus.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:
He spoke, and addressed Antinous winged words:

Antinous, truly you care for me well as a father for a son,
398	you who bid the stranger be driven from the hall
399	with a word of compulsion; may a god not bring that to pass.
400	Take something and give it; I do not begrudge it; I bid you myself;
401	do not spare my mother in this, nor any other
402	of the servants who are in the house of divine Odysseus.
403	But you have no such thought in your breast;
404	for you wish much more to eat yourself than to give to another.
And Antinous answered him in turn and said:

Telemachus, high-talker, unrestrained in fury, what have you said.
407	If all the suitors would give him so much,
408	the house would keep him away for three months.
So he said, and took the footstool from under the table,
which lay there, on which he rested his sleek feet when feasting;
and all the others gave, and filled his wallet
with bread and meat; and soon Odysseus was about
to go back to the threshold and taste the Achaeans' gift;
but he stood by Antinous, and spoke a word to him:

Give, friend; you seem to me not the worst of the Achaeans
416	but the best, since you are like a king.
417	Therefore you should give even better than the others
418	of bread; and I would spread your fame over the boundless earth.
419	For I too once dwelt in a house among men,
420	prosperous and rich, and often gave to a wanderer,
421	whoever he was and whatever need he came with;
422	and I had servants, very countless, and many other things
423	by which men live well and are called rich.
424	But Zeus son of Kronos destroyed it—for he wished it, I suppose—
425	who sent me with roving pirates
426	to go to Egypt, a long journey, that I might perish.
427	And I stopped the curved ships in the river Egypt.
428	There indeed I bade my trusty comrades
429	stay there by the ships and guard the ships,
430	and I urged scouts to go to the lookouts.
431	But they, yielding to insolence, following their own strength,
432	at once began to ravage the very beautiful fields of the Egyptian men,
433	and carried off women and infant children,
434	and killed the men; and soon the cry reached the city.
435	And they, hearing the shout, came at dawn
436	appearing; and the whole plain was filled with foot-soldiers and horses
437	and the flashing of bronze; and Zeus who delights in thunder
438	cast evil panic on my comrades, nor did any dare
439	to stand firm to face them; for evils stood round on every side.
440	There they killed many of us with the sharp bronze,
441	and others they led up alive to work for them under compulsion.
442	And me they gave to a stranger who met them, to Cyprus,
443	to Dmetor son of Iasus, who ruled mightily over Cyprus;
444	and from there I now come here, suffering woes.
And Antinous answered him in turn and said:

What god brought this plague, this grief of a feast?
447	Stand so in the middle, away from my table,
448	lest soon you come to a bitter Egypt and Cyprus;
449	what a bold and shameless beggar you are.
450	You stand beside all in turn; and they give
451	heedlessly, since there is no restraint or pity
452	in being generous with others' goods, since each has much.
And withdrawing, wise Odysseus said to him:

Alas, so there was no sense in you to match your looks;
455	you would not give even salt from your own house to your suppliant,
456	you who now sitting at another's table did not dare to take
457	a bit of bread and give it to me; yet there is much by you.
So he spoke, and Antinous was more angry at heart,
and looking darkly at him spoke winged words:

Now I think you will no longer go back fair
461	out of the hall, since you speak insults too.
So he spoke, and took the footstool and hit him on the right shoulder,
at the very base of the back; and he stood like a rock,
steadfast, nor did Antinous's missile make him stagger,
but silently he shook his head, brooding evil in his mind.
Going back to the threshold he sat down, and set down his wallet
full, and spoke among the suitors:

Hear me, suitors of the very famous queen,
469	that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me.
470	There is indeed no grief in the mind nor sorrow,
471	when a man is struck while fighting for his own possessions,
472	for his cattle or his white sheep;
473	but Antinous struck me for the sake of my wretched belly,
474	accursed, which gives many evils to men.
475	But if there are gods and Furies of beggars anywhere,
476	may the end of death come upon Antinous before his marriage.
And Antinous, son of Eupeithes, said to him:

Eat at ease, stranger, sitting, or go elsewhere,
479	lest the young men drag you through the house, for what you say,
480	by foot or hand, and flay you all over.
So he spoke, and all of them were exceedingly indignant;
and so one of the arrogant young men would say:

Antinous, you did not well to strike the unlucky wanderer,
484	accursed man, if there is some god in heaven.
485	For gods too, in the likeness of strangers from foreign lands,
486	taking every shape, go about the cities,
487	watching the insolence and the good order of men.
So the suitors spoke, but he paid no heed to their words.
And Telemachus nursed great grief in his heart
at the blow, but did not let a tear fall to the ground from his eyelids,
but silently shook his head, brooding evil in his mind.
And when prudent Penelope heard of him
being struck in the hall, she spoke among her maidservants:
So may famous-bowed Apollo strike you yourself.
And the housekeeper Eurynome answered her with a word:

If only our prayers might be fulfilled;
497	not one of these men would reach fair-throned Dawn.
And prudent Penelope answered her:
So she spoke among her women servants,
sitting in her chamber; and divine Odysseus dined;
and she called the divine swineherd to her and said:

Go, divine Eumaeus, and bid the stranger
509	come, so that I may greet him and ask
510	whether he has heard anything of patient Odysseus or has
511	seen him with his eyes; for he looks like one who has wandered much.
And answering her you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

If only, queen, the Achaeans would be silent;
514	such things he tells that your dear heart would be charmed.
515	For three nights I had him, and for three days I kept him
516	in the hut; for he came to me first, escaping from a ship;
517	but he has not yet finished the story of his woes.
518	As when a man gazes at a singer, who, taught from the gods,
519	sings words delightful to mortals,
520	and they long unceasingly to hear him, whenever he sings,
521	so he charmed me, sitting by me in the halls.
522	He says he is a guest-friend of Odysseus from his father's time,
523	dwelling in Crete, where is the race of Minos.
524	From there he has now come here, suffering woes,
525	rolling onward; and he declares he has heard of Odysseus
526	near, in the rich land of the Thesprotian men,
527	alive; and he brings many treasures to his house.
And prudent Penelope answered him:

Go, call him here, that he may tell me face to face.
530	And let these men either sit at the doors and make merry,
531	or here in the house, since their heart is glad.
532	For their own goods lie untouched in their houses,
533	bread and sweet wine; these their servants eat,
534	while they frequent our house all days,
535	sacrificing cattle and sheep and fat goats,
536	and feast and drink the gleaming wine,
537	heedlessly; and the most is consumed. For there is no man,
538	such as Odysseus was, to ward off ruin from the house.
539	But if Odysseus came and reached his fatherland,
540	quickly with his son he would take vengeance on the violence of men.
So she spoke, and Telemachus sneezed loudly, and the house
rang terribly around; and Penelope laughed,
and at once spoke to Eumaeus winged words:

Go, call the stranger here before me.
545	Do you not see that my son sneezed at all my words?
546	Therefore death will not be unaccomplished for the suitors,
547	for all of them, nor will any escape death and doom.
548	And another thing I shall tell you, and lay it in your mind:
549	if I find he tells all truly,
550	I shall clothe him in a cloak and tunic, fair garments.
So she spoke, and the swineherd went, when he heard the word;
and standing near spoke winged words:

Stranger father, prudent Penelope calls you,
554	the mother of Telemachus; her heart bids her
555	ask something about her husband, though she has suffered griefs.
556	And if she finds you tell all truly,
557	she will clothe you in a cloak and tunic, which you most
558	need; and bread you will feed your belly
559	begging through the land; and whoever wishes will give you.
And much-enduring divine Odysseus answered him:

Eumaeus, quickly I could tell all truly
562	to the daughter of Icarius, prudent Penelope;
563	for I know well about him, and we have endured the same misery.
564	But I am afraid of the throng of harsh suitors,
565	whose violence and force reach the iron heaven.
566	For even now, when this man, as I went through the house
567	having done no harm, struck me and gave me pain,
568	neither Telemachus prevented it, nor anyone else.
569	Therefore now bid Penelope in the halls
570	to wait, however eager, until the sun goes down;
571	and then let her ask me about her husband's day of return,
572	seating me nearer by the fire; for I have wretched clothes;
573	you know yourself, since I first begged of you.
So he spoke, and the swineherd went, when he heard the word.
And as he crossed the threshold, Penelope addressed him:

You do not bring him, Eumaeus; what is this the wanderer has in mind?
577	Does he fear someone excessively, or is he otherwise
578	shy in the house? A shy wanderer is a bad one.
And answering her you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

He speaks rightly, as another too would think,
581	avoiding the insolence of the arrogant men.
582	But he bids you wait until the sun goes down.
583	And for you yourself it is much better, queen,
584	to speak to the stranger and hear him alone.
And prudent Penelope answered him:
So she spoke, and the divine swineherd went
to the throng of the suitors, when he had told her everything.
At once he spoke to Telemachus winged words,
holding his head close, so that the others should not hear:

Friend, I am going to guard the swine and what is there,
594	your livelihood and mine; and let all here be your care.
595	First save yourself, and consider in your heart
596	lest you suffer harm; many of the Achaeans think evil,
597	whom may Zeus destroy before woe comes to us.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:
So he spoke, and he sat again on the well-polished seat,
and having satisfied his heart with food and drink
he went to the swine, and left the courts and the hall,
full of feasters; and they delighted in dancing and song;
for already the evening day had come.
